Where it began

Trent Boult was born in Rotorua on 22 July 1989 and grew up in Ōhope and Tauranga, going to school at Ōtūmoetai College. Cricket ran in the family: his older brother, Jono Boult, played the game too.

His boyhood hero was Wasim Akram, which tells you most of what you need to know about the bowler he became. He played at the Under-19 World Cup in Malaysia in 2008, and at 19 he was already in a New Zealand one-day squad, where he turned out to be the quickest bowler on the tour.

The player

His Test debut came at Hobart in December 2011, and it was a good one to remember. He took four wickets as New Zealand won by seven runs, their first Test win in Australia since 1985. Over the next decade he played 78 Tests and took 317 wickets at 27.50, with ten five-wicket hauls.

There were plenty of big days. At the Basin Reserve against the West Indies he took ten wickets in the match, 10 for 80. In Auckland in 2018 he took six as England were bowled out for 58, and he was named player of that series. He reached 300 Test wickets against Bangladesh in January 2022, and he was part of the side that won the 2019–2021 World Test Championship.

What made him special

He was not especially tall, but he made up for it with deceptive pace and swing both ways, above all the ball that curved back into a right-hander. With Tim Southee he formed a long and fruitful new-ball partnership, and for years the pair took a large share of New Zealand's wickets. He was also known for one-handed diving catches, taken with either hand.

In white-ball cricket he shone as well. He was the joint top wicket-taker at the 2015 World Cup and, in 2019, became the first New Zealander to take a hat-trick at a World Cup. He was also in the New Zealand sides that reached the World Cup finals of 2015 and 2019.

Away from the middle

He was in demand in the Indian Premier League. In 2020 he helped Mumbai Indians win the title, took the match award in the final and was named player of the season. After leaving international cricket in 2024, he carried on in Twenty20 leagues around the world. At home he won the Sir Richard Hadlee Medal for New Zealand's best international player in 2018.

And finally

Batting at the bottom of the order, he finished not out in 46 of his 94 Test innings, so opposing bowlers often found a way past everyone else before they found one past him. He made 759 Test runs, and one fifty, which shows he could hit the ball when he chose to.
